passages.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Fact Sheet & Patient Education
passages.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that affects women of reproductive age, with an estimated prevalence of 8% to 13% worldwide. It is characterized by hormonal imbalances, irregular or absent ovulation, higher-than-normal levels of androgens (male-type hormones), and small fluid-filled follicles (sac-like structures) in the ovaries. Irregular periods alone do not confirm PCOS; clinical assessment by a healthcare professional is required.

passages.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Fact Sheet & Patient Education
passages.text: Symptoms of PCOS vary from person to person and may change over time. Common symptoms include heavy, long, intermittent, unpredictable, or absent menstrual periods (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea); excess facial or body hair (hirsutism); persistent acne or oily skin; scalp hair thinning or male-pattern baldness; weight gain especially around the abdomen; difficulty conceiving (infertility due to irregular ovulation); and darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans) associated with insulin resistance.

passages.title: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome 2023
passages.text: While the genetic predisposition to PCOS cannot be prevented, healthy lifestyle management is recommended for all individuals with PCOS to improve metabolic, reproductive, and psychological health and reduce long-term risks such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Evidence-based habits include regular physical activity (at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening exercises twice weekly), a balanced nutrient-dense diet rich in fiber, whole grains, lean proteins, fruits, and vegetables, adequate sleep hygiene, and stress reduction. No single specific diet outperforms a balanced healthy eating pattern.

passages.title: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome 2023
passages.text: In adults (18 years and older), clinical evaluation for PCOS typically uses the revised Rotterdam criteria, which require at least two of the following three features after excluding other conditions (such as thyroid disorders or hyperprolactinemia): (1) irregular or absent ovulatory cycles, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or elevated anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels as assessed by a clinician.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.locator: Section 1: What is Menstruation & Normal Cycle Range
passages.text: Menstruation is the normal monthly shedding of the uterine lining (endometrium) driven by cyclical changes in reproductive hormones (estrogen, progesterone, LH, and FSH). In adults, a typical menstrual cycle ranges from 21 to 35 days, with menstrual bleeding lasting between 2 and 7 days. Menstrual irregularities include cycles shorter than 21 days (polymenorrhea), longer than 35 days (oligomenorrhea), absent periods for 3 or more months (amenorrhea), or abnormally heavy bleeding (menorrhagia).

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.locator: Section 2: Menstrual Symptoms & When Cycles Change
passages.text: Common menstrual symptoms include mild-to-moderate lower abdominal or pelvic cramping (primary dysmenorrhea caused by uterine prostaglandins), lower back ache, breast tenderness, bloating, headache, fatigue, and premenstrual mood changes. Symptoms that interfere with daily activities, sudden changes in cycle regularity, bleeding between periods, or soaking through one or more pads or tampons every hour for two consecutive hours warrant medical evaluation.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.text: General lifestyle habits that support healthy menstrual function and help reduce mild menstrual discomfort include regular aerobic physical activity, applying a warm heating pad or taking a warm bath to relax uterine muscles, staying well hydrated, consuming iron-rich foods (such as leafy greens, legumes, and lean meats) paired with vitamin C to prevent iron deficiency from menstrual blood loss, maintaining consistent sleep, managing stress, avoiding smoking, and practicing safe menstrual hygiene by changing menstrual products regularly.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.text: Seek immediate emergency medical care if menstrual or pelvic symptoms are accompanied by: soaking through 1 or more sanitary pads or tampons every hour for 2+ consecutive hours; severe, sudden, or worsening lower abdominal or pelvic pain; dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting (syncope), or shortness of breath; possible pregnancy combined with vaginal bleeding or one-sided pelvic/shoulder pain (to rule out ectopic pregnancy); or high fever and chills with pelvic pain or foul-smelling discharge.

passages.title: ACOG Clinical Consensus: General Approaches to Medical Management of Menstrual Pain and Dysmenorrhea
passages.locator: Section 1: Definition of Primary vs Secondary Dysmenorrhea
passages.text: Dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation that impairs daily functioning. Primary dysmenorrhea refers to recurrent, crampy lower pelvic pain that occurs with menses in the absence of demonstrable pelvic disease, mediated by elevated endometrial prostaglandin production. Secondary dysmenorrhea is menstrual pain associated with an underlying pelvic pathology, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, or uterine fibroids.

passages.title: ACOG Clinical Consensus: General Approaches to Medical Management of Menstrual Pain and Dysmenorrhea
passages.text: Symptoms of primary dysmenorrhea typically begin shortly before or with the onset of menstrual flow and peak within 24 to 48 hours. Pain is characteristically spasmodic or dull, localized in the lower abdomen or suprapubic region, and may radiate to the lower back and anterior thighs. Associated systemic symptoms commonly include nausea, fatigue, loose stools or diarrhea, headache, and dizziness.

passages.title: ACOG Clinical Consensus: General Approaches to Medical Management of Menstrual Pain and Dysmenorrhea
passages.text: Evidence supports several non-pharmacologic lifestyle strategies for managing mild-to-moderate menstrual cramping. Continuous topical heat therapy (applying a warm heating pad or patch to the lower abdomen) has been shown in clinical trials to be as effective as standard analgesics in reducing cramping intensity by relaxing uterine smooth muscle. Regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling for 30 minutes, 3 to 5 times weekly), adequate sleep, stress-reduction techniques, and smoking cessation also significantly diminish menstrual symptom severity.

passages.title: CDC Public Health Guide: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (Menorrhagia) and Iron Deficiency
passages.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding (historically termed menorrhagia) is defined clinically as menstrual blood loss greater than 80 mL per cycle or bleeding that lasts longer than 7 consecutive days. In practical everyday terms, heavy bleeding is identified when flow soaks through one or more sanitary pads or tampons every hour for two or more consecutive hours, requires wearing double protection, or interrupts routine daily life and sleep.

passages.title: CDC Public Health Guide: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (Menorrhagia) and Iron Deficiency
passages.text: Symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding include passing blood clots larger than a quarter (one inch in diameter), having to wake up during the night to change menstrual protection, bleeding for longer than a full week, and signs of secondary iron-deficiency anemia such as persistent tiredness, lethargy, pale skin, unexplained weakness, cold hands or feet, and shortness of breath with mild exertion.

passages.title: CDC Public Health Guide: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (Menorrhagia) and Iron Deficiency
passages.text: To prevent iron deficiency caused by heavy menstrual blood loss, dietary strategies include regularly eating iron-rich foods (heme iron from lean poultry and fish, or non-heme iron from lentils, beans, spinach, and fortified cereals) consumed together with vitamin C sources (such as citrus fruits, bell peppers, or tomatoes) to boost intestinal iron absorption. Avoid consuming calcium-rich foods, tea, or coffee simultaneously with iron-rich meals because polyphenols and calcium inhibit iron uptake. Keeping a detailed menstrual diary tracking pad counts and cycle dates assists clinicians in identifying treatable causes.

passages.title: WHO Fact Sheet: Endometriosis Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Supportive Care
passages.text: Endometriosis is a chronic disease where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (endometrium) grows outside the uterus, most commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, outer uterine surface, and pelvic peritoneum. This ectopic tissue responds to monthly hormonal cycles by thickening, breaking down, and bleeding, but has no exit path from the body, leading to chronic inflammation, scarring, fibrosis, and adhesions. It affects approximately 10% (190 million) of reproductive-age girls and women globally.

passages.title: WHO Fact Sheet: Endometriosis Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Supportive Care
passages.text: The primary symptom of endometriosis is severe, progressive pelvic pain. Symptoms include intense menstrual cramping (dysmenorrhea) that does not respond to standard over-the-counter pain relievers; chronic, non-menstrual pelvic pain throughout the month; deep pain during or after sexual intercourse (dyspareunia); painful bowel movements or painful urination especially during menstrual periods; heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding; fatigue; and difficulty getting pregnant (subfertility).

passages.title: WHO Fact Sheet: Endometriosis Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Supportive Care
passages.text: While there is currently no known primary prevention or permanent cure for endometriosis, supportive non-pharmacological care significantly improves quality of life. Helpful lifestyle habits include consuming a nutrient-dense, anti-inflammatory eating pattern rich in omega-3 fatty acids, colorful vegetables, and antioxidant-rich berries; engaging in gentle, low-impact exercise (such as yoga, walking, and gentle stretching); working with a specialized pelvic floor physical therapist; practicing relaxation and mindfulness techniques to down-regulate centralized pain sensitivity; and using thermal heat therapy during flare-ups.
